harvest:
You go down and work with them. By midday there are marks on your hands. This is not your trade, and nobody says so.

{n} units in.

Eleven people in the fields today. Your part is the counting and the sorting out: who goes to which plot, and when they change over.

Counted at dusk: {n} units. Old Wendt says that at this rate it will do.

Halfway through the cutting a fine rain starts and nobody stops. It is not much rain, and stopping only makes you colder.

{n} units. The wheat is damp; it was spread out to dry overnight.
fell_timber:
Three to a team, and you go with the one furthest out. The sound of axes carries a long way in the woods, and every so often there is the dull noise of one going down.

{n} units. {r} left of this year’s allowance.

Mostly you spend the day marking: which come down and which do not. Marking is more tiring than cutting, because there is no going back on a wrong one.

{n} units.

One of the logs jammed among the roots on the way out and took four men half an hour.

{n} units. It was dark by the time the work stopped.
survey_fields:
You walk every plot of it. Which ripens fastest, which hollow holds water, whose bank has fallen away at a corner.

You know these things now. It produces no figure at all, and the next time you have to decide something you will use it.

You meet two tenants on the easternmost plot. They stop and say a few things to you. Not a report — talk. They say the weather this year is not what it was last year.

You hear them out. They look a little surprised that you heard them out.

You walk the bank to the end of it and turn round, and the whole of it lies out below you.

For the first time you see plainly how large this estate is.
survey_forest: You take the north path. The spacing of the trees, the thickness of them, whether any are sick. You do not really know how to read it, but you write down what you see.

There is fog in the woods today. Some way in you look back, and there is nothing to see in the direction of the estate.

You stand where you are a while before you go on.

Below a slope you find old cutting. Not this year’s; the faces have gone black. Two or three years back at least.

You write down where.
forest_state: No light gets into the woods. The canopy closes overhead, and a quarter of an hour in you still cannot see the slope opposite. The leaf litter is soft underfoot: last year’s below it, and the year before that below that.

There are a few places with light in them now. You stop at them; the stumps are new and the saw cuts are paler than the bark. The wood is still thick, but you can make out which lines through it are yours.

You can see from this side to the other now. The trees that are left stand far enough apart that the wind goes through without resistance. The litter is much thinner, and in places the bare earth shows.
This slope is open now. Standing in the middle of it you can see the sky, and the ridge opposite, and which channels the water will take when it rains. The soil is loose and gives under your feet.
stable_help:
You go to the stable to help. Gregor does not tell you what to do. He hands you a brush and points at the far stall.

Brushing a horse is harder work than you thought. With the coat, even pressure, and where it has knotted you do not pull.

Halfway through you look up and find him watching you from the other end. He looks away.

Today it is hooves. Gregor does one for you to watch, taking the leg up between his own knees and working the hook out along the frog.

“Not the middle,” he says.

Three words, and that is all of them. You do six, and you never once touch the cleft down the middle.

You are changing the bedding. The old straw has to be shaken out and looked over for mould, and the new goes down packed but not packed dead.

Nobody taught you this. You watched him do it three times and worked it out.

When it is done he comes over and looks, says nothing, and straightens the one bundle you had put down crooked.
repair:
The smith was brought out from Valehold for the day. You worked alongside him, which mostly meant handing things over and paying for them.

{item} — done.

It was more trouble than you thought. Once it was open there was a second thing broken inside, and that cost more.

{item} — done. It came to a little over what you had put aside.

Gregor came over, looked at it, said two sentences and went. Done his way it went a great deal easier.

{item} — done.
forage:
The strip along the edge of the woods has come up well this year. Martha knows these things; she drew you a rough chart of them once.

Turned into {n} guldmark.

You gathered all morning and brought it back for Martha to look at. She picked out half and said the other half was not to be eaten.

What was left made {n} guldmark.

Not much about today. The season for it is nearly over.

{n} guldmark.
orchard:
The orchard has not been properly pruned in years and the fruit is small. Small fruit is sweet.

You picked all morning.
Children from two of the tenant households came to help, and each took a few away with them when it was done. You did not stop them.

What is too high cannot be reached, and that fruit comes down of itself and rots on the ground. It is like this every year.

Martha says it is not waste. What falls rots into the soil, and next year the tree bears better.
office_paperwork:
A morning of papers. Copies of contracts, the tenant roll, last year’s harvest record, several letters nobody ever answered.

Elena came in twice. The first time with water, the second to take away what needed washing.

Neither time did she make a sound.

You are sorting last year’s files. One stack has an even edge — not the evenness a stack falls into, but the kind that comes of somebody squaring it sheet by sheet.

Elena is wiping the shelves by the window. When you look up she has just lowered her head.

Halfway through the papers you notice that the inkwell has been moved, to where your right hand comes to it more easily.

You did not ask anyone to move it.
night_ledger_1:
The ledger at night is not the ledger by day.

By day you are looking at whether the figures come out. At night there is nothing else to be done, so you begin to look at other things. Who wrote a note in the margin, and on which page. Which entry was changed and then changed back. Which month is written tighter than the months around it.

Hartmann kept it for eight years. Eight years is a great many pages.
night_ledger_2:
You start at the earliest volume and work forward.

The first years are clean. The columns are clear, the summaries written out in full, and here and there a correction, every one of them initialled.

He was in his twenties then.

By the fourth year the lamp needs filling.
night_ledger_3:
What you are looking for is not a figure.

You lay the eight years out on the desk in order and open every one of them at the same month. October. The harvest. Eight Octobers.

The first seven Octobers are written the same. Neat, evenly spaced, the strokes of the numbers finished off clean.

The eighth is not.

It is not careless. You would have seen careless long ago.

It is small.

The same ruled boxes, the same columns, and the writing nearly a third smaller than it was through the seven years before, crowded up into the top left of each box, with a wide space left empty at the right.

You set the seventh volume and the eighth side by side and look at them for a long time.

What has to happen to a man before his handwriting gets smaller.

It is not a shaking hand and it is not failing eyes. The strokes are steady and the ends are still clean.

He was only taking up less and less room.
rest:
You did nothing at all today.

Slept until you woke, sat two hours in the forge-chapel in the afternoon, went to bed early.

Getting up the next morning, you realise it has been a very long time since you last had enough sleep.
You stayed in your room the whole day. That pale rectangle on the desk. You looked at it a long while.

You sat in the stable all afternoon. Gregor did his work and you sat. Neither of you said anything.

Nothing at all moved forward today. You find you do not mind.
stable_help_third:
When you have finished and are about to go, he takes a brush down off the rack and holds it out to you.

Not the one he was using; that one is in his hand. This one has a shorter handle and has been used longer.

“This one sits better,” he says.

You take it. You do not know what to say, and he does not wait for you to say it.

When you come back the next day the brush is on a hook by the door, hung apart from the other tools, on its own.
night_ledger_4:
You sat with it another night.

The eight volumes are the same eight volumes. You know by now what there is to look for, and it is not the figures, and it is no longer the handwriting either.

You only sit here, turning the pages of what one man wrote over eight years.

When the lamp is half burned down you close the ledger.

You have finished with this.
